episode.title: The UN Monitoring Team's latest report: Where the global jihad stands now

organizations.name: United Nations Monitoring Team
aliases: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
organizations.notes: 10 independent experts; dual mandate (UNSCR 1267 on al-Qaeda/ISIL; UNSCR 1988 on Afghanistan/Taliban); two 1267 reports per year (written June/December), one 1988 report per year (last Nov, next planned Oct 2026); word limit cut from 10,600 to ~9,000; reports by consensus; lowest-ever member-state engagement on the last Afghanistan report.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: UN: >25,000 fighters globally under AQ and affiliates, ~two-thirds in Africa; ransom money moved JNIM -> AQIM -> AQAP and AQ central leadership, showing a functioning global network; debate among agencies whether AQ is a 'consultancy', regional, or a global org awaiting its moment.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: UN: >16,000 fighters, ~two-thirds in Africa; 'at a lower ebb'/'on the ropes': lost deputy leader Abu Khadija (2025) and successor al-Maynuki (May 2026); leadership dispersed and isolated; spokesman statement 'drenched in blood'.

organizations.name: ISKP
organizations.notes: Pioneering use of crypto financing, adopted by other groups.

organizations.name: TTP
organizations.notes: UN notes a very high number of claimed attacks in Pakistan in 2026 — an intensification not getting attention; Fitton-Brown frames it as a war between Taliban-controlled Afghanistan and Pakistan.

events.description: UN Monitoring Team's 1267 report (written June 2026) released, covering ISIL and al-Qaeda.
Reported ~$50 million ransom payment to JNIM (reported in the previous UN report, end of 2025).
JNIM katibas attack Bamako, Kidal and Kati; Mali's defense minister killed in a massive suicide car bomb in Kati; financed by the ransom.
Ransom funds flowed from JNIM to AQIM, then to AQAP and al-Qaeda central leadership — evidence of a global AQ network.
Islamic State spokesman al-Ansari's first statement in ~2 years, downbeat: past years 'drenched in blood'.
Unconfirmed reports that al-Ansari was killed in a special forces operation in Yemen (day of recording).
Islamic State deputy leader Abu Khadija killed; replaced by al-Maynuki (head of al-Furqan office, West Africa).
Al-Maynuki killed in a US-Nigerian operation.
Operation Hilaac by Somali/Puntland forces drives IS-Somalia's Mumin into hiding in the Cal Miskaad mountains.
Uptick in TTP attacks in Pakistan; very high number of claimed attacks.
Syrian government forces take control of al-Hol and other NE Syria camps; 130 holes found in al-Hol walls; 15-20,000 unaccounted for.
13 Daesh drone trainers travelled from the Middle East to ISWAP; first ISWAP armed drone attacks followed within months.
Last UN 1988 (Afghanistan) report; lowest member-state engagement ever; next planned ~Oct 2026.

sources_cited: UN Monitoring Team 1267 report on ISIL and al-Qaeda, released Aug 2026 (written June 2026)
UN Monitoring Team report, end of 2025 (JNIM $50M ransom)
UN Monitoring Team 2024 report (13 Daesh drone trainers to ISWAP)
key_claims: Al-Qaeda numbers >25,000 fighters globally and Islamic State >16,000, about two-thirds of each in Africa; Africa is the main growth theatre, but South Asia (TTP attacks in Pakistan) is intensifying and under-reported.

The flow of a ~$50M ransom from JNIM to AQIM, then to AQAP and al-Qaeda's central leadership, shows al-Qaeda still functions as a global network capable of transferring resources — against the view that it is merely a 'consultancy' or regional.
Islamic State is 'at a lower ebb': deputy leader Abu Khadija killed (2025), successor al-Maynuki killed (May 2026), Mumin in hiding, leadership dispersed, spokesman's statement downbeat.
Member-state engagement on Afghanistan is at its lowest ever; the 1988 report is being de-prioritized even as TTP violence surges — a trend the Monitoring Team finds concerning.
15,000-20,000 people from al-Hol and other NE Syria camps are unaccounted for after Syrian government forces took over (130 holes in al-Hol's walls).

Budget cuts shrank the Monitoring Team's reports from 10,600 to ~9,000 words, reducing fidelity; the South Asia section in the latest 1267 report was thinner because material is held for the next Afghanistan report.
Counter-terrorism remains an area of Security Council consensus despite wider divisions.
